items.title: Gemini 4 Neon: the middle model built for agents
items.explainer: Neon is a new Gemini 4 model adapted from Google's larger Carbon model and tuned to balance depth and cost, with a 1 million token context window. Google says it costs 32% less per task than Carbon and charges $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. On Google's own benchmark table it leads on long-document search and office automation tasks and roughly ties rivals elsewhere.
items.why: If the mid-priced model now does the work of the flagship, the default advice for schools and small teams is to start with the cheaper tier and test.

items.title: Five daily AI uses for learning design, each with its own check
items.explainer: A learning designer audited a year of her own chats and found her use shifted from doing things faster to doing them better. Her five uses run from analysing every learner comment by category to building a feedback bot from your own edited drafts. Each one ends with a verification step, such as marking every quote as verified, paraphrased or not found.
items.why: Her rule, AI reads and counts and the human decides, is a ready-made frame for faculty workshops.

items.title: A public speed dashboard for running models on your own AMD hardware
items.explainer: The llama.cpp project now publishes weekly benchmarks of local models on AMD Ryzen and Radeon chips. It reports two numbers: how fast a model reads a 512 token prompt and how fast it writes 128 tokens, each repeated 10 times. Those two numbers decide whether a local model feels usable on a laptop.
items.why: Local models keep student text off the cloud, and this gives a neutral way to check whether a given machine can run one.

tryThisWeek.title: Run your next quiz past three synthetic students
tryThisWeek.steps: Paste 5 to 10 questions from an upcoming quiz into any chatbot without the answer key and ask it to predict how a beginner with common misconceptions, a middle learner and an expert would answer, with the reason for each answer. Then paste the key and ask it to flag questions that are too easy, too hard, unclear or have weak distractors. Treat the beginner's answers with caution: the author notes AI is poor at playing weak learners.

hook: On one overall score two top AI models sit two points apart. How far apart are they when asked to find things in a million-token document?

lead.title: The middle model that outscored the flagships
lead.dek: Google's Gemini 4 Neon, a cheaper model adapted from its biggest one, tops its rivals on Google's own table, and the gaps are widest where the work is long and messy.
paragraphs: Gemini 4 Neon arrived on November 18 as the middle of three Gemini 4 models: Carbon for the hardest long projects, Hydrogen for fast everyday work, and Neon in between. It is adapted from Carbon, reads up to 1 million tokens at once, and costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Google says it uses 32% less money per task than Carbon at its default setting.

The headline overall score is close: 61 for Neon against 59 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 57 for GPT-6.2 Sol on the Artificial Analysis index. The gaps open on specific jobs. On GraphWalks, a test of following links through 256,000 to 1 million tokens of text, Neon scores 95.2% against 66.8% and 80.1%. On AutomationBench, a test of office automation tasks, it scores 56.3% against 42.5% and 41.3%.

That pattern matters more than the rank. An overall index averages away the differences that decide whether a model fits a job, such as reading a full course archive or a semester of feedback in one pass. Early users have praised it too; the fast.ai founder Jeremy Howard called it really good at teaching, as quoted in one widely read weekly roundup.
lead.against: Every number here comes from Google's own model card, chosen and run by Google, and on several tests the rivals are within a point or two or ahead. Google also skipped a full new safety evaluation for Neon, carrying forward results from an earlier model because the capability jump fell under its own threshold.
lead.watch: Independent leaderboards over the next two weeks, and whether the long-document lead holds when teachers and researchers test it on their own files.
lead.ask: Which of your courses has a long pile of text, a semester of journals or feedback, where a model that reads all of it at once would change what you could notice?

graph.title: Close on average, far apart on the long read
graph.tease: Google's model card for Gemini 4 Neon scores it against Claude Opus 5.5 on the same tests.
graph.question: On the overall index they are 2 points apart. On finding things across 256,000 to 1 million tokens of text, how far apart are they?
graph.reveal: The gap on the long read is 28.4 points, fourteen times the overall gap. An average score hides the job-specific differences that decide which model fits a task.
graph.caveat: All scores are self-reported by Google on its own model card; they are not independent tests, and other benchmarks on the same card show the two models within a point.

argue.claim: The bigger risk of AI writing in school is not cheating; it is that everyone starts to sound the same.
argue.context: A widely shared quote describes a "great de-individualization": the same model voice in videos, conference talks and pitch emails. If that is the cost, voice becomes the thing worth grading.
argue.source: Simon Willison, quoting Jack Despain Zhou
